articles.title: Frances Tiafoe and Ayan Broomfield’s relationship: From young tennis players to a decade of love and support
articles.summary: International Sports News: Frances Tiafoe and Ayan Broomfield’s relationship has grown alongside his tennis career. What started with a meeting through a mutual friend in 2015 h.
articles.body: Frances Tiafoe and Ayan Broomfield’s relationship has grown alongside his tennis career. What started with a meeting through a mutual friend in 2015 has turned into a decade-long partnership filled with big wins, difficult moments, travel and plenty of memories.Broomfield has been there through some of the biggest moments of Tiafoe’s career, often watching from the player’s box and sharing the emotions that come with life on the ATP Tour.2015: Frances Tiafoe and Ayan Broomfield’s relationship beginsFrances Tiafoe and Ayan Broomfield met through a mutual friend in 2015, when they were both young tennis players. Tiafoe was starting to make his mark in professional tennis, while Broomfield was building her own path in the sport.Their relationship became public later that year. In December, Tiafoe shared a sweet Instagram post about Broomfield and wrote about missing her during the holidays.At the time, neither knew just how much their lives would change in the years ahead.2017–2019: Frances Tiafoe and Ayan Broomfield grow closer togetherIn 2017, Tiafoe celebrated their second anniversary with a loving tribute to Broomfield. A year later, they spent Valentine’s Day together in France, with Broomfield describing Tiafoe as her partner and best friend.Their careers were also moving forward. In 2019, Tiafoe traveled to Los Angeles for Broomfield’s UCLA Senior Day. That same year, she and Gabby Andrews won the NCAA women’s doubles championship.Tiafoe proudly celebrated her achievement, showing that their support has always gone both ways.2020–2021: Frances Tiafoe and Ayan Broomfield’s life beyond tennisTheir relationship continued to grow away from the court too. In 2020, they celebrated Broomfield’s 21st birthday.Then came King Richard. Broomfield worked as a tennis body double for Venus Williams in the movie’s tennis scenes, putting her own tennis experience to work on the project. Tiafoe joined her at the film’s Los Angeles premiere in November 2021.It was another moment where their personal and professional worlds came together.2022: Ayan Broomfield supports Frances Tiafoe through his US Open breakthroughThe 2022 US Open changed Frances Tiafoe’s career forever.He defeated Rafael Nadal and Andrey Rublev before reaching the semifinals, where he pushed Carlos Alcaraz to a thrilling five-set match. Broomfield was there as he experienced the biggest run of his career at that point.Speaking to the ATP Tour, she later called those two weeks “magical” and said the experience changed their lives and the lives of Tiafoe’s family.She also explained why they work so well together. Tiafoe is naturally happy-go-lucky, while she is more serious and grounded. That difference, she said, helps them balance each other.2023–2024: Frances Tiafoe and Ayan Broomfield celebrate career milestones togetherWhen Tiafoe broke into the ATP top 10 in 2023, Ayan Broomfield celebrated the achievement online. She revealed that she had saved screenshots of his milestones, waiting for the day he would reach that level.Tiafoe responded by thanking her for staying beside him through “the good, the bad and the standstills.”In 2024, she continued supporting him at major tournaments, including Wimbledon and the US Open. During the US Open, she sat beside Tiafoe’s mother in the player’s box, holding hands and sharing the tension of his matches.Away from tennis, the couple continued making memories, including a 2024 Kansas City Chiefs game where they met Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce.2025–2026: Frances Tiafoe and Ayan Broomfield remain by each other’s sideAfter nearly a decade together, Broomfield remains one of the most familiar faces in Tiafoe’s corner.She continues to attend tournaments, cheer for him and use humor to make the pressure of tennis a little lighter. Tiafoe, meanwhile, has repeatedly celebrated her as his “rock” and someone he is deeply thankful to have in his life.As another US Open approaches, their story feels especially meaningful. Broomfield has seen Tiafoe before the fame, before the biggest wins and before the pressure that comes with being one of America’s top tennis stars.She has been there through all of it. And perhaps that is what makes their relationship so special, not simply that they have celebrated the highs together, but that they have continued choosing each other through every stage of the journey.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: How did Elena Rybakina build her $20 million fortune? The incredible rise that made her one of tennis' biggest earners
articles.summary: International Sports News: Elena Rybakina has turned a quiet personality and powerful tennis game into a fortune estimated at $20 million. Her wealth did not arrive overnight. I.
articles.body: Elena Rybakina has turned a quiet personality and powerful tennis game into a fortune estimated at $20 million. Her wealth did not arrive overnight. It grew through years of grinding on the professional circuit, major Grand Slam success and a growing list of commercial partnerships. From a young player facing financial limits to one of tennis' biggest stars, Rybakina's rise has been both remarkable and highly rewarding.Elena Rybakina's $20 million fortune grew with Grand Slam successRybakina's biggest financial breakthrough came with her 2022 Wimbledon triumph. At just 23, she defeated Ons Jabeur in the final to become the first player representing Kazakhstan to win a Grand Slam singles title. The victory changed her status in tennis and gave her career a powerful commercial lift.But Wimbledon was only the beginning. Rybakina followed it with a run to the 2023 Australian Open final and then captured WTA 1000 titles at Indian Wells and Rome. Her ability to compete across hard courts, clay and grass helped turn her into a regular contender at the biggest tournaments.Her prize money accelerated sharply as her results improved. According to Celebrity Net Worth, Rybakina has collected more than $30 million in official tournament prize money during her career, which is already greater than the site's estimated $20 million net worth. That difference highlights an important point: career earnings and net worth are not the same thing.The 2025 WTA Finals delivered one of her most remarkable paydays. Rybakina went unbeaten through the tournament and defeated world No. 1 Aryna Sabalenka in the final. Her perfect 5-0 campaign earned her $5.235 million, described by the source as a record prize for a women's professional sporting event at the time.Her momentum continued into 2026. Rybakina won her second Grand Slam at the Australian Open, defeating Sabalenka in a dramatic three-set final. She later won Stuttgart again and reached her first US Open final. That run also secured her rise to world No. 1 for the first time.Elena Rybakina's endorsements add another major income streamTournament winnings are only one part of Rybakina's financial success. Her profile has also attracted major brands, particularly after her Wimbledon breakthrough.Her endorsement portfolio has included Yonex, Red Bull, Lexus, Bank RBK, KAZ Minerals, Fanatics, Topps and Swiss watchmaker Vanguart. Yonex has been especially visible, providing her racquets, clothing and footwear.Rybakina's appeal is interesting because she has never relied heavily on a loud public persona. Her calm approach on court has become part of her identity. Instead, her biggest selling point is performance. Grand Slam titles, deep tournament runs and a world No. 1 ranking have steadily increased her value to sponsors.Her journey also adds another layer to the story. Born in Moscow, Rybakina switched to representing Kazakhstan in 2018 after the country's tennis federation offered financial and developmental support. That backing helped give her the stability needed to pursue elite tennis.Today, the combination of prize money, sponsorships and years of success has helped establish Rybakina as one of the highest-earning names in women's tennis. Her estimated $20 million fortune reflects not just one breakthrough, but the financial rewards of building a sustained career at the very top of the sport.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Roger Federer built an $8.1 million glass mansion on Lake Zurich; after listing his Wollerau villa for $5.3 million, he sold it as plans grew for a massive new waterfront compound
articles.summary: International Sports News: Roger Federer’s former Wollerau home near Lake Zurich was one of his most striking properties, but the Swiss tennis great eventually put the glass res.
articles.body: Roger Federer’s former Wollerau home near Lake Zurich was one of his most striking properties, but the Swiss tennis great eventually put the glass residence on the market as his plans changed. The three-story home, known as “The Residence,” covered about 500 square metres and included large glass walls, balconies, a pool and underground parking. Federer reportedly listed the property for 5.4 million Swiss francs, about $5.3 million, in 2017. It was sold the following year. By then, Federer had already moved his Swiss base to Valbella and was looking toward a much larger waterfront project in Rapperswil-Jona.What did Roger Federer’s $8.1 million Wollerau glass mansion includeFederer’s Wollerau home stood in the canton of Schwyz, on the shores of Lake Zurich. He had the modern property built as a family home, with the project completed around 2014. Architectural Digest India reported that the house was worth about £6.5 million at the time and had three levels with around 500 square metres of space.The design was built around the lake view. Floor-to-ceiling glass brought in plenty of natural light, while large balconies looked out toward the water. The property also had a swimming pool and underground parking.The home was not only for Federer, his wife Mirka and their four children. A separate living space was also planned for his parents, Robert and Lynette. That made the property more than a luxury house for the tennis star; it was designed to keep his wider family close while giving everyone their own space.Why did Roger Federer put his Wollerau villa up for saleFederer’s plans for Wollerau changed over time. He had already moved his official residence to Valbella in the Swiss canton of Graubünden in 2015. In 2017, the Wollerau property was put up for sale, with the asking price reported at 5.4 million Swiss francs.The exact final sale price was not publicly confirmed. Local reports said the property was eventually bought by a wealthy person from the canton of Zurich, who worked in the wealth-management sector. The sale was reported in July 2018.That detail matters because the $5.3 million figure refers to the reported asking price or estimated value, not a confirmed final transaction price. The Bote der Urschweiz reported that the actual amount paid was not known, although it was believed to be around that level.How did Roger Federer’s Rapperswil-Jona property change his plansWhile Federer was leaving Wollerau, another Lake Zurich project was taking shape. In 2018, he acquired a large waterfront property in Kempraten, part of Rapperswil-Jona. The site covers roughly 16,000 to 18,000 square metres, depending on how the property area has been reported. Swiss reports placed the land’s value at around 40 million to 50 million Swiss francs.The new project was far larger than the Wollerau home. Plans included several buildings, a tennis court and sports facilities, with the property giving the Federer family direct access to Lake Zurich.The project has not moved as quickly as originally expected. Construction has faced objections and disputes linked to the waterfront, environmental issues and access along the lake. Swiss public broadcaster SRF reported in 2019 that the building permit had been approved, while later reports showed that the project continued to face delays.By August 2025, Swissinfo reported that construction was moving ahead. The site was then described as almost 17,000 square metres, with several buildings under development. The report also said that the family had originally hoped to move there in 2021.What is planned for Roger Federer’s new Lake Zurich estateThe Rapperswil-Jona property is meant to give Federer and his family much more room than the old Wollerau residence. Reports have described a group of buildings rather than one single villa, along with a tennis court and indoor sports facilities.Le Temps reported in 2024 that the property covered more than 16,000 square metres and that Federer was building about half a dozen structures there. The report estimated the land purchase at around 50 million Swiss francs, with another 20 million francs expected in construction costs.There is also a planned boat facility, although that part of the project has faced a separate dispute. The Swiss federal authorities challenged approval for the boat shelter, according to Le Temps.The scale of the project shows why the Wollerau house no longer fit Federer’s plans. Instead of one three-story residence on a relatively small plot, the new property gives his family a much larger private space on the lake.Where does Roger Federer’s Swiss and global property portfolio standFederer still has strong links to several parts of Switzerland. His Valbella properties in the Lenzerheide area have been part of his Swiss real estate holdings, while his Rapperswil-Jona project has become his biggest known residential development.He also owns property in Dubai. Architectural Digest reported that Federer has a luxury penthouse in the Le Reve tower in Dubai Marina, with the property estimated at about $23.5 million.Federer has also sold other Swiss property over the years. In 2024, Blick reported that he sold a roughly 5,800-square-metre plot in Herrliberg, another location on Lake Zurich.That makes the Wollerau sale part of a wider change in Roger Federer’s property holdings. The glass home was built as a high-end family residence during his playing career, but within a few years he had sold it and shifted his attention to a much bigger waterfront project in Rapperswil-Jona.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: US Open 2026 results: How Alexander Zverev turned tears into triumph in New York
articles.summary: How a more composed Alexander Zverev stayed 'zen-like' to beat Ben Shelton and win the US Open, six years after a heart-breaking defeat in the final.
articles.body:
As he stepped up to the baseline, Alexander Zverev could be forgiven for letting his mind slip back to the last time he served for the US Open title.

Six years ago, the German top seed threw away a two-set lead in a devastating loss to Dominic Thiem, having served for the match in the fifth set.

This time, instead of his own nerves, it was American Ben Shelton and the majority of the 24,000-strong crowd that stood in Zverev's way.

But this was a different Zverev: a Grand Slam champion now, having won the French Open in June.

Such was his focus that he did not initially realise he had sealed a 6-3 7-6 (7-2) 5-7 6-2 victory.

After firing down another unstoppable serve to win the match, Zverev returned to the baseline ready to start the next point - only to be told by his team the match was over.

"In that moment I was in the zone a lot. I didn't hear noise at all," Zverev said.

"It's funny - tennis teachers always tell you to just play the next point and forget about the score.

"At that moment I forgot about the score and it helped me."

As the realisation sunk in, the 29-year-old broke into a broad and slightly surprised smile before raising his arms above his head.

It was a direct contrast to his defeat by Thiem in 2020, where a tearful Zverev said during the trophy presentation: "I wish one day I can bring the trophy home."

"We went 30 years without winning a Grand Slam title and now we've won two in three months," said Zverev.

"2026 is the outcome of all the years that happened before."

Zverev's parents were not there for his previous final at Flushing Meadows, but his father and coach Alexander senior was on the sidelines this time.

As well as paying tribute to his father, Zverev also thanked his mother for her support following his type 1 diabetes diagnosis as a child.

"When doctors tell you that life and sports will be very limited for that child, it takes a very strong mother to say 'my son will be whatever he wants to be'," Zverev said.

"My mother is the most important and strongest person I know."

Zverev caps transformational year with US Open triumph

All About US Open: Zverev claims second Grand Slam title

World number two Zverev has enjoyed his best year on the Tour, reaching the semi-finals at the Australian Open and the final at Wimbledon alongside his French Open and US Open successes.

He has been aided by injuries to Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz, who swept the majors in the past two seasons, but a strengthened mentality and dedication to fitness has also helped.

"There is no-one as fit as Zverev, he is right up there," former Wimbledon champion Marion Bartoli said on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"You can argue about Alcaraz and Sinner, and Novak [Djokovic] and Rafa [Nadal] when they were in their prime physically, but Zverev is right up there as one of the best athletes to play the sport."

Zverev was taken to five sets in his first two matches, with both finishing in the early hours of the New York morning.

He was two points from defeat in the first round, but rallied, played his way into form and did not drop a set from the third round until the final.

Faced with a partisan crowd against Shelton, Zverev did not buckle. He kept his emotions deliberately in check and, even though he lost the third set, never loosened his grip on the match.

"I'm so admiring of his strength of character and the zen-like state he's been in since the very beginning of the match," said former British number one Annabel Croft.

"The most extraordinary thing - and I don't think I've ever witnessed it - was that he didn't realise he had won.

"It was so bizarre, but it was like he was in a trance-like state while he was playing."

His serve - one of the best on the ATP Tour - was key against Shelton.

He won 39 of 42 points behind his first serve in the first two sets and did not face a break point until the middle of the third.

Shelton broke at the end of the third set to extend the match but the American made little impact in return games from then on, winning only four of 20 receiving points in set four

Victory means he will now have the world number one ranking in his sights - he trails Sinner by 1,810 points with two Masters 1000 events and the season-ending ATP Tour finals to come.

But Zverev is a polarising figure in tennis.

In October 2023, he was given a penalty order and fined 450,000 euros (£392,000) for bodily harm against his ex-partner, with whom he shares a child.

Zverev denied the claims and lodged an objection against the order. A trial in May 2024 was discontinued after a week and there was a separate settlement between Zverev and his ex-girlfriend.

At the time, the court told BBC Sport: "The decision is not a verdict and it is not a decision about guilt or innocence."

Zverev was also accused in October 2020 of physical violence and controlling behaviour by another former girlfriend. He maintained his innocence from the start and there were no legal proceedings.

articles.title: US Open: Ben Shelton suggests rule change over champion Alexander Zverev's ball-bouncing habit
articles.summary: The 2026 US Open will go down as a triumph for Alexander Zverev. With some grumbles along the way.
articles.body:
The 2026 US Open will go down as a triumph for Alexander Zverev. With some grumbles along the way.

The German defeated Ben Shelton 6-3, 7-6, 5-7, 6-2 on Sunday to capture his second career Grand Slam title, a few months after his first such trophy at Roland-Garros. It was a brilliant performance , especially on a serve Shelton only managed to break once across four sets.

That serve perturbed many opponents this tournament, but not just because of its 130-plus mph speeds and the backhand often following it. It was also the waiting.

Throughout the tournament, Zverev kept opponents on indefinite standby with his serve. There is a 25-second serve clock in between points for exactly this reason, but no such limit exists on second serves.

So Zverev was seemingly bouncing the ball upward of 10 times on every single second serve. Sometimes in excess of 20 times. It bothered his opponents, the crowd and the broadcasters, with everyone speculating what could be done about it.

That includes Shelton, who suggested a a time limit for second serves while speaking with reporters after the match :

"For a first serve you should be able to do whatever you want and use the full 25 seconds every time. I think that there should be some sort of rule — I'm not sure exactly how you would do it — limiting time on second serves. You shouldn't have unlimited time. For our sport, for the fans. I think it's tough to be sitting there for that long for the next action to happen. "I'm sure at some point it will be something that these tournaments look at just because there is such a delay in play in some matches."

"For a first serve you should be able to do whatever you want and use the full 25 seconds every time. I think that there should be some sort of rule — I'm not sure exactly how you would do it — limiting time on second serves. You shouldn't have unlimited time. For our sport, for the fans. I think it's tough to be sitting there for that long for the next action to happen.

"I'm sure at some point it will be something that these tournaments look at just because there is such a delay in play in some matches."

The ball-bouncing was addressed at one point in Sunday's match. The chair umpire gave Zverev a time violation in the fourth set after such a delay, to the loud delight of the Arthur Ashe Stadium crowd. Zverev appeared to argue he was actually waiting for a crowd clearly partial to Shelton to settle down.

Karen Khachanov, Zverev's semifinal opponent, had a similar issue with the ball bounces in their match but conceded it was within the rules:

"The way he bounces the ball, look, it annoys not only me, of course, but a lot of players, because it takes so much time. You don't know how to prepare for the serve. You are ready, and then it's another 12 bounces. "Every point like that. At the end of the day, if it's within the rules with the time between points, I cannot say anything against that, because it's within the rules. If he extends the time, he gets a time violation, so it's pretty simple as that."

"The way he bounces the ball, look, it annoys not only me, of course, but a lot of players, because it takes so much time. You don't know how to prepare for the serve. You are ready, and then it's another 12 bounces.

"Every point like that. At the end of the day, if it's within the rules with the time between points, I cannot say anything against that, because it's within the rules. If he extends the time, he gets a time violation, so it's pretty simple as that."

This stuff isn't particularly new with Zverev — you can see him bounce the ball 12 times before his first second serve in this 2026 Australian Open match — but the number of bounces definitely seemed to increase in this tournament. It is also the kind of scrutiny players start experiencing once they become multi-time Grand Slam champions.

For his part, Zverev insisted he's not trying to reach a specific number and said he actually did try to decrease the bounces while speaking with reporters after the semifinal:

"I'm not counting in my head. I'm not getting a certain number or anything like that. I don't know why it increased so much. Today it decreased again, because I saw it before the semifinals so I was like, 'OK, it's gotta go less,' but then I forget about it every once in a while and it goes up. I don't know what number it is.

"I'm not counting in my head. I'm not getting a certain number or anything like that. I don't know why it increased so much.

Today it decreased again, because I saw it before the semifinals so I was like, 'OK, it's gotta go less,' but then I forget about it every once in a while and it goes up. I don't know what number it is.

Whatever is done about the ball-bouncing, 2026 stands to go down as a career season for Zverev. He entered the year as the consensus best player to never win a Grand Slam and proceeded to go 25-2 in Grand Slams that year, losing to only Carlos Alcaraz (Australian Open semifinal) and Jannik Sinner (Wimbledon final).

Questions remain about his ability to beat modern tennis' new duopoly, but it's clear his legacy has changed this year.

articles.body: Trinity Rodman made a 200-mile trip from Washington to New York on Sunday after playing for Washington Spirit, arriving at Arthur Ashe Stadium in time to watch boyfriend Ben Shelton lose the US Open final to Alexander Zverev.Rodman was playing for the Washington Spirit against Boston Legacy at almost the same time as Shelton's first Grand Slam final, making it difficult for her to get to New York. articles.summary: Tennis News: Alexander Zverev had waited six years to erase the pain of his first US Open final. When the moment finally arrived, the German did not even realise h.
articles.body: Alexander Zverev had waited six years to erase the pain of his first US Open final. When the moment finally arrived, the German did not even realise he had won it.Zverev defeated American Ben Shelton 6-3, 7-6(2), 5-7, 6-2 on Sunday to win his first US Open title and second Grand Slam of the year, following his maiden major triumph at Roland Garros in June. But after sealing the championship point, the world No. 2 remained behind the baseline, preparing to receive another serve.It took his team’s reaction — and a glance around the stadium — for Zverev to realise that he was now a US Open champion.‘I didn’t hear that she said, Game, set, match’Zverev said he was so locked into the contest that he completely missed the chair umpire announcing the end of the match.“In that moment, I was in the zone a lot. I didn't hear noise at all,” Zverev said during his post-match press conference. “I was in this kind of tunnel where I just didn't hear anything. Also, when the crowd is loud, it's impossible to hear the umpire, so I didn't hear that she said, ‘Game, set, match’. At the end of the day, I just forgot the score. I just thought it was 5-1 instead of 6-2.”The victory was particularly significant for Zverev, who had lost the 2020 US Open final to Dominic Thiem after leading by two sets and being two points from the title.The German believes those scars have now finally disappeared.“I think the scars of the 2020 final, they kind of disappeared after I won in Paris,” Zverev said. “I said it at Wimbledon. Even though I lost the final, I enjoyed the match. I enjoyed being in the Grand Slam final, I enjoyed playing on Centre Court, and I enjoyed playing in front of an amazing crowd, in front of some celebrities and all that. I enjoyed doing that.”“Whereas before winning in Paris, I felt a lot of stress all the time, because there was always a question mark: ‘Will I ever win one?’ What I think now is just more of a joy to play those kinds of finals.”Zverev’s verdict on SheltonShelton was playing in his first Grand Slam final, but Zverev was impressed by how much the 23-year-old had developed.“I think he's very talented, but he's very close to the hard work as well,” Zverev said. “You see him and his father all the time after matches, before matches, working on different things, and every single year he keeps improving something.”“I just played him today. I think this was the best backhand he's ever hit against me, the most consistent power. There was everything there.”Zverev recalled their first meetings and said Shelton had added a new level of consistency to his game.“I remember a couple of years ago when I first played him, he was always dangerous, he always had that serve, and he always had that forehand. But if you played three, four balls back, there would be an error, and that was absolutely not the case today.”‘Right, right now, probably yes’Zverev’s second major of the season also put him in a unique position in 2026. He is the only player to have won multiple Grand Slam titles this year, while Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz have won one each.Asked whether he now considers himself the best player in the world, Zverev was reluctant to make an absolute claim — but conceded that, at this particular moment, he may have the strongest case.“I don’t know how to answer that,” he said. “You have to take everything into consideration. With Jannik Sinner being injured, Carlos Alcaraz coming back from injury after four months, right now, this moment, probably yes."“Both of them healthy, both of them at the top of their game? Maybe not. But if we say right, right now, with Jannik being injured and Carlos coming back from injury, maybe.”Sinner missed the US Open through injury, while Alcaraz returned to Grand Slam action in New York after a four-month injury layoff.Zverev, however, was quick to acknowledge that the hierarchy could look very different when all three are fully fit.“Four or five months ago, when both of them were healthy, I wasn’t [the best player in the world],” he said. “I was losing to Jannik all the time. If everyone is healthy, I think Jannik is still ahead. It’s as simple as that,” he added.Zverev is 0-5 against Sinner this year, having won just one set against the world No. 1 — a tiebreaker in the Wimbledon final.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.summary: Tennis News: Last time none of Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic were in the top 10 of the ATP rankings, George W Bush was the US president, euro had .
articles.body: Last time none of Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic were in the top 10 of the ATP rankings, George W Bush was the US president, euro had just entered circulation, and Ronaldo had just led Brazil to the FIFA World Cup title.For the first time since October 2002, the men's top 10 no longer includes any member of the Big Three. Djokovic, the last active player from the trio, dropped from No. 5 to No. 12 in the latest ATP rankings released on Monday after his early exit at the US Open.Federer retired in 2022 at the age of 41, while Nadal retired in 2024 at 38. Djokovic, now 39, is the last member of the trio still playing.The rankings underline how much tennis has changed. In October 2002, Lleyton Hewitt was the world No. 1. Nearly 24 years later, his 17-year-old son Cruz Hewitt is now beginning his own professional career.Djokovic's fall came after a first-round defeat to Mariano Navone at the US Open. It was his earliest Grand Slam exit in 20 years, dating back to the 2006 Australian Open, and the first time he had lost his opening-round match at the US Open."I've been very proud of all the achievements in the past, but now is now," Djokovic said after the defeat in New York.Djokovic remains the most successful men's singles player in Grand Slam history with 24 major titles, ahead of Nadal's 22 and Federer's 20.The numbers behind the Big ThreeFederer entered the ATP top 10 later in October 2002 and stayed there until the end of 2016. During that period, he also spent a record 237 weeks as world No. 1.Nadal broke into the top 10 in April 2005 during his rise on clay as an 18-year-old. He stayed in the top 10 for a record 912 consecutive weeks before dropping out in 2023.Djokovic entered the top 10 in 2007 and went on to spend a record 428 total weeks as world No. 1.A new generation takes overThe current rankings continue to be led by Jannik Sinner, Alexander Zverev and Carlos Alcaraz.This season has been very different from last year. Sinner and Alcaraz met in three of the four Grand Slam finals in 2025, but they did not face each other in any major final in 2026.Alcaraz missed both the French Open and Wimbledon because of a right wrist injury, while Sinner withdrew from the US Open with a right knee injury.While Alcaraz won the Australian Open and Sinner won Wimbledon, the most consistent player this season has been Zverev. He won the French Open and the US Open, finished runner-up at Wimbledon and reached the semifinals of the Australian Open.Even after winning his second Grand Slam title of the year, Zverev stopped short of calling himself the world's best player.“If everyone is healthy, I think Jannik is still ahead,” Zverev said after beating Ben Shelton in the US Open final. “It's as simple as that.”Ben Shelton, after reaching his first Grand Slam final at the US Open, climbed five places to world No. 4 in the latest rankings.Rybakina replaces Sabalenka at No. 1On the women's side, Elena Rybakina moved to world No. 1 after winning her second Grand Slam title of the season at the US Open, having also won the Australian Open earlier this year.Rybakina's victory ended Aryna Sabalenka's run of 99 consecutive weeks as world No. 1.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2009, Juan Martin del Potro beat Roger Federer to win the US Open for Argentina; 17 years later, he remains the last non-European Grand Slam winner
articles.summary: Tennis News: There was a time when men's Grand Slam tennis had champions from across the globe. Australia, the United States, Argentina and South Africa all produc.
articles.body: There was a time when men's Grand Slam tennis had champions from across the globe. Australia, the United States, Argentina and South Africa all produced major winners, adding different styles and stories to the sport's biggest tournaments. But the landscape has changed dramatically.Juan Martin del Potro's historic 2009 US Open triumph remains the last time a non-European man won a Grand Slam singles title. The Argentine defeated five-time defending champion Roger Federer in a five-set final at Flushing Meadows, producing one of the biggest upsets of his career. More than 17 years later, that victory still stands as the most recent men's singles Grand Slam title won by a player from outside Europe.Since then, the men's Grand Slam scene has been dominated almost entirely by European stars. Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic drove the first part of that era, before the next generation led by Carlos Alcaraz, Jannik Sinner and Alexander Zverev continued the trend.The numbers make the change particularly striking. From 2010 through 2026, every completed men's singles Grand Slam has been won by a European player. The only exception in terms of a tournament not having a champion was Wimbledon in 2020, which was cancelled because of the COVID-19 pandemic.From the Big Three to Alcaraz, Sinner and ZverevFederer, Nadal and Djokovic were responsible for much of Europe's extraordinary dominance during the 2010s. Nadal repeatedly ruled Roland-Garros, Djokovic collected titles at the Australian Open, Wimbledon and US Open, while Federer continued to add major trophies.Andy Murray of Great Britain also broke through during this period, winning Wimbledon twice and the 2012 US Open. Switzerland's Stan Wawrinka, Croatia's Marin Cilic and Austria's Dominic Thiem were among the other Europeans to lift Grand Slam trophies.The transition to the next generation has not changed the geographical pattern.Spain's Alcaraz won the 2026 Australian Open, completing a career Grand Slam at just 22 years old. He became the youngest man to win all four major singles titles.Germany's Alexander Zverev then captured his maiden Roland-Garros title in 2026 before adding the US Open trophy yesterday in New York. articles.title: Toby Samuel: Brit to make Davis Cup debut after 'surreal' year
articles.summary: Briton Toby Samuel is to make his Davis Cup debut for Great Britain after what he calls a "surreal" 12 months.
articles.body:
Toby Samuel says it was "one of the best moments in my life" when he was selected in Great Britain's Davis Cup team to face Ecuador this weekend after a breakthrough year.

The 23-year-old was handed his maiden Davis Cup call-up after a rapid rise over the past 12 months, climbing into the top 100 in the world rankings and making his debut in three Grand Slams.

"It's surreal being in this position now from where I was eight, nine months ago, [when I was] hopefully trying to play some Challengers, and now I'm sat here ready to play the Davis Cup - it's crazy," he told BBC Points West.

Samuel joins Arthur Fery, Cameron Norrie, Henry Patten and Lloyd Glasspool in the squad to face Ecuador at London's Copper Box arena.

Samuel breaks more new ground with first win at a Slam

Fery named in GB Davis Cup team to face Ecuador

Samuel, who is from Winchester and trains in Bath, was in New York having just made his US Open debut when he was told the news.

"I was out in New York walking around when I got a call up from Leon [Smith] the captain saying, 'congratulations, you've been selected,'" Samuel added.

"It was unbelievable, it was one of the best moments of my tennis life, to get called up to that, it's what every British player wants, to represent their country and play for their country."

At the US Open, Samuel claimed his first victory in a Grand Slam with a dominant win over Tomas Machac before losing to 18th seed Jiri Lehecka in the next round.

It has been a year of firsts as Samuel also reached the main draw of the French Open, coming through three rounds of qualifying before losing to world number eight Alex de Minaur in the first round proper.

Weeks later, he was handed a wildcard entry at Wimbledon and took Czech 15th seed and French Open semi-finalist Jakub Mensik to five sets.

"At first it was a completely new experience, I was pretty nervous going to those tournaments, seeing the top guys there in the locker rooms and playing against them - I was sort of shaking a little bit on court," Samuel said.

"But after the second or third time I did it I got more used to it and I felt like I was a lot calmer on the court, which helped me to go deep."

Stepping up to the top-tier tournaments has meant mentally and physically there has been a lot for Samuel to learn this past year.

With Challenger Tour matches played over three sets, this is the first time Samuel has consistently played five-set matches.

Being able to play for three, four or even five hours is a "new thing", although he feels his serve and forehand have improved significantly.

"Before they were good but they weren't really scaring people," he said. "Now they're my biggest weapons and I can take matches with them."

articles.title: Atlanta’s Ben Shelton bid to be 1st American winner of US Open since 2003 ends in loss to Zverev
articles.summary: With history on the line for the US Open, Ben Shelton falls short of bringing home the win for America. He'd aimed to be the first American to win since 2003...
articles.body:
Ben Shelton had already told the fans he was really going to need them.

"I'm gonna need you guys on Sunday to bring the energy," the American had told a cheering Arthur Ashe Stadium crowd when he beat compatriot Frances Tiafoe in the U.S. Open semifinals, setting up his first Grand Slam final. "We're going for it here."

Well, Shelton sure had Sunday's crowd. As opponent and ultimate victor Alexander Zverev himself correctly estimated, "99.9%" of the crowd seemed to be supporting Shelton.

The brashly confident and appealing 23-year-old was trying to become the first American to win a Grand Slam title since Andy Roddick won the U.S. Open in 2003 — and the first Black man to win the tournament since Arthur Ashe in 1968.

But with all that history on the line — and maybe even because of it — it wasn't enough.

Shelton fell to a far more accurate and experienced Zverev, 6-3, 7-6 (2), 5-7, 6-2, as the hard-serving German extended what has been a stellar year in which he's captured two Grand Slams and come close to knocking Jannik Sinner off his world No. 1 perch.

It cheered Shelton, the No. 8 seed, constantly — from the moment he arrived on court, and whenever he exhibited intermittent flashes of brilliance. "Let's go Ben!" they chanted, and sometimes "USA! USA!" Especially in the third set, when Shelton prevailed. The crowd roared, and settled in for a change of direction.

But it didn't happen. Zverev quickly broke for a 2-0 lead, then broke again for 5-2, and won the match more quickly than many anticipated — apparently including Zverev, who didn't realize at first that he'd actually won.

Minutes later, at the trophy ceremony, a downcast Shelton recovered to smile and then charm the crowd, thanking everyone from, first, God, to his family and his team, and down to his driver and "the security guards who make me smile every day."

He saved his final thanks for the fans of New York, especially those "who stayed until 4 in the morning." That was a reference to his epic quarterfinal win over No. 2 seed Carlos Alcaraz in a five-set thriller that will be talked about for years — and only partly because it concluded at 3:33 a.m., the latest finish ever at the Open.

Speaking to the media later Sunday, Shelton was subdued, but clearly focused on the future.

"I'm motivated," he said. "Disappointed with how today went (but) happy with how I fought throughout the week, two weeks. Excited with the progress that I feel that I've made, but yeah, this one stings 100%.

"It's on to the next," he said. "Try to keep getting better and show up in Australia even stronger than I showed up here."

If Shelton had been troubled by the weight of history and the dreams of a long-denied tennis nation, he did not mention it.

But earlier in the week, he seemed to consciously downplay that angle.

"Like, yes, I can think about how cool this moment is and what I'm playing for," he had said after his semifinal. "But at the end of the day, I'm here in New York, I'm hanging out with my team, I'm with my homies playing a little bit of tennis, and I've been able to downplay the moment pretty well."

Asked Sunday what had made the final against Zverev so challenging, he first cited the incredible accuracy of the German's serve.

"He's got the best serve in tennis," Shelton said. "I broke him today for the first time in 66 games. I think you combine that with as good as he is as a tennis player outside the serve, how complete he is, he's gotten so much better at the net. He's an elite mover at 6-foot-7. He's got a lot of length, so he returns really well. Solid from the baseline and one of the fittest guys on tour too."

And he noted his own lack of consistency.

"I definitely didn't execute from the ground the way I wanted to," he said. "I didn't hit my forehand well today … I made too many errors, and I think that's the big piece from me. I want to be more lethal with my forehand."

Shelton also made clear he was annoyed with how many times Zverev was bouncing the ball before serves — a practice that even brought Zverev some boos from the crowd, as when he sought to complain about a time violation issued by the umpire.

Shelton said the umpire had told him to get to the line earlier to return serve. "I was, like, 'He can start his routine whenever he wants. I promise you there will never be a time where he serves and I'm not ready. But I shouldn't have to sit at the line — you know, if he's bouncing the ball 20 to 25 times, I shouldn't have to just sit there for that."

Summing up his experience in the biggest match of his life, though, Shelton made clear he was focusing on the positives.

"It's such a cool moment," he said. "Walking out on that court today, there's nothing like it. I've never felt anything like that before. It's an addicting feeling being in positions like this."

"Obviously for me it sucked the last couple of Grand Slams sitting at home for 10, 11, 12 days while the tournament was still going on, watching everyone else run through the draw. You know, it's motivating. Losing in the final is also motivating, but this is the position I want to be in."

And he made clear he knows he needs to keep improving.

"I don't think I'm anywhere near the player that I want to be," Shelton said. "I think I'm a great competitor. ... But yeah, to win on Sundays, you've got to play a very, very high level of great tennis.

articles.standfirst: La salida de Djokovic, único miembro activo en el circuito, cierra un ciclo de más de dos décadas
articles.summary: La salida de Djokovic, único miembro activo en el circuito, cierra un ciclo de más de dos décadas
articles.body: Corren tiempos de cambio por las calles de la vieja guardia. Por primera vez en 24 años, ningún miembro del 'Big 3': Novak Djokovic, Rafa Nadal y Roger Federer, aparece en el top10 del ranking ATP. La reciente salida del serbio, único miembro de los tres tenistas en activo, es la respuesta. Su derrota en la primera ronda del US Open ante Navone, le ha hecho caer desde el quinto hasta el decimosegundo puesto. El suizo y el español, retirados en 2022 y 2024, respectivamente, han visto esta semana al último miembro del exitoso grupo de los 66 Grand Slam salir de la cima compuesta por los 10 mejores tenistas del mundo más de dos décadas después. El 14 de octubre de 2002 es la fecha de inicio de este dominio ininterrumpido en el top10 del ranking. Fue cuando un joven de 21 años nacido en Basilea, llamado Roger Federer, ingresó por segunda vez en estas posiciones. Se mantuvo hasta el 7 de noviembre de 2026, acumulando 734 semanas consecutivas. Por su parte, Rafa Nadal hizo su primera aparición (con 18 años) en este exclusivo grupo el 25 de abril de 2005, hasta el 6 de marzo de 2023, fijando su marca en un récord de 912 semanas. El último en unirse a los 10 primeros fue, el todavía presente en el circuito, Novak Djokovic. El 19 de marzo de 2007 inicio su periplo de 553 semanas hasta el 6 de noviembre de 2017, ahí permaneció nueve meses fuera del top10. Regresó el 20 de agosto de 2018 para continuar por 421 semanas más, hasta hoy. Los tres mayores ganadores de la historia coincidieron dentro del top10 en dos periodos. El primero, durante 503 semanas (casi 10 años). Marca su inicio la fecha de entrada del serbio (19 de marzo de 2003) hasta la primera salida del suizo (17 de noviembre de 2016). El segundo periodo ocurre entre el 16 de julio de 2018 y el 18 de octubre de 2021, fecha en la que Roger Federer dejó de pertenecer a la élite. Durante 673 semanas (no consecutivas) el 'Big 3' coincidió entre los 10 mejores jugadores del mundo.

articles.title: Inspiring story on fatherhood: “Becoming a father has changed me; I want to set a good example” – how Alexander Zverev’s daughter inspired him to become a better man on and off the tennis court
articles.summary: International Sports News: Alexander Zverev has opened up about how becoming a father changed the way he sees himself, especially when it comes to his behavior on and off the te.
articles.body: Alexander Zverev has opened up about how becoming a father changed the way he sees himself, especially when it comes to his behavior on and off the tennis court. The German tennis star became a father to his daughter, Mayla, in 2021, and says the experience has given him a different sense of responsibility. Zverev has always been an emotional player, and his frustration has sometimes been visible during matches. But he now looks at those moments differently because he knows his daughter will one day see how he handled them. When Zverev said, “Becoming a father has changed me; I want to set a good example,” he was not simply talking about becoming calmer during tennis matches. He was talking about the kind of person he wants to be for his daughter and the values he hopes she will see in him as she grows up.What did Alexander Zverev mean when he said fatherhood changed him?Alexander Zverev’s comment was mainly about responsibility. Before becoming a father, his focus was largely on himself, his career and his results. Like any top athlete, he wanted to win, and losing could bring out strong emotions. He has had moments on the court when his frustration got the better of him, including angry outbursts and racket-smashing incidents.But becoming a father gave him something bigger to think about.Now, Zverev is not only thinking about what happens when he wins or loses a match. He is also thinking about the person his daughter will see when she looks at him. That can change the way someone reacts to difficult situations.His words suggest that he does not want Mayla to grow up seeing him as someone who lets anger control him. Instead, he wants her to see a father who can deal with pressure, disappointment and difficult moments without losing control.That does not mean Zverev suddenly stopped being emotional. Tennis is still an intense sport, and he remains a passionate competitor. The difference is that he has become more aware of how he handles those emotions.For him, fatherhood has added another reason to keep improving as a person.Why is setting a good example so important to Zverev?When Alexander Zverev talks about setting a good example, he is thinking about much more than tennis.Children often learn by watching their parents. They notice how their parents react when things go wrong, how they treat other people and how they handle pressure. Zverev appears to understand that his daughter will learn from what he does, even when he is not directly teaching her anything.That is why his own behavior matters to him.Zverev has spoken about wanting to be remembered not only for what he achieved on a tennis court but also for the person he was away from the sport. That is an important part of his comment about fatherhood.Winning major tournaments can define an athlete’s career, but Zverev knows that his daughter will not judge him only by the number of trophies he wins. For her, he is simply going to be her father.That gives his words a different meaning.He wants Mayla to be proud of him not just because he is a successful tennis player, but because he tries to be a good person. His work away from tennis also matters to him, including his efforts through the Alexander Zverev Foundation, which supports children living with Type 1 diabetes.So, setting a good example is about his whole life. It is about showing his daughter that success is not only about winning. It is also about how you treat people, how you deal with setbacks and what you do when nobody is keeping score.Has fatherhood changed the way Zverev handles his emotions?This is probably one of the clearest ways to understand his quote.Zverev has never hidden the fact that he can be emotional on the court. Tennis can be frustrating because players are often alone with their thoughts for several hours. One mistake can change a match, and the pressure is even greater when a major title is at stake.Earlier in his career, Zverev sometimes struggled to control that frustration. His emotions could become a major part of his matches.However, he has made an effort to change that side of himself.Zverev has pointed out that he had not smashed a racket for several years, showing that he has become better at controlling his anger. While that change cannot be credited only to fatherhood, becoming a parent has clearly given him another reason to work on himself.There is also a bigger lesson behind this.Being a role model does not mean being perfect. Zverev can still get frustrated. He can still have bad days. What matters is how he responds when things do not go his way.That is something he can eventually pass on to his daughter.He wants her to understand that losing is not the end of the world and that making mistakes is part of life. What matters is picking yourself up and trying again.In that sense, controlling his emotions is not only helping Zverev as a tennis player. It is also part of the person he wants to become as a father.What kind of example does Zverev want to set for his daughter?At the heart of Zverev’s quote is a simple idea: he wants his daughter to see the best version of him.His career will continue to have wins and losses. There will be tournaments where everything goes right and others where nothing seems to work. But those results will eventually become part of the past.The example he sets for Mayla can last much longer.Zverev wants her to see someone who works hard for what he wants but also understands that life is bigger than tennis. He wants to show her how to deal with pressure without allowing it to change who you are.He also wants his actions away from the court to matter. His charity work, his relationship with his family and the way he carries himself are all part of the legacy he wants to build.For Zverev, fatherhood has therefore brought a new kind of motivation. He is still competing for titles and trying to reach the top of tennis, but there is now someone watching him who matters in a completely different way.That is what makes his statement about becoming a father so meaningful.“Becoming a father has changed me” is not simply about his life changing after Mayla was born. It is about realizing that his choices can influence someone else. And when he says, “I want to set a good example,” he is saying that he wants his daughter to grow up seeing a man who learns from his mistakes, controls his emotions, treats people well and keeps trying to become better.For Zverev, that may ultimately be one of the most important things he can leave behind.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Frances Tiafoe now has the opportunity to achieve a career first after his impressive US Open campaign
articles.summary: Frances Tiafoe has enjoyed the best season of his career to date. The rejuvenated American star has performed at a high level throughout the year,...
articles.body:
Frances Tiafoe has enjoyed the best season of his career to date.

The rejuvenated American star has performed at a high level throughout the year, as evidenced by his title-winning campaign in Halle and his impressive run to the US Open semi-finals.

Tiafoe defeated Valentin Vacherot, Daniil Medvedev and Alex Michelsen en route to the last four in New York, before losing to compatriot Ben Shelton in four sets.

Consequently, Tiafoe has now achieved a career-high ranking of world number eight.

The American has also given himself the opportunity to qualify for an iconic tournament for the first time in his career.

Frances Tiafoe can qualify for the ATP Finals

Tiafoe has never competed in the ATP Finals .

Players qualify for the end-of-year event by earning one of the eight best ranking points total across the year.

Tiafoe – who earned 800 ranking points in New York – has now moved up two places to sixth in the 2026 race, overtaking Arthur Fils and Daniil Medvedev.

The American still trails Alexander Zverev, Jannik Sinner, Ben Shelton, Carlos Alcaraz and Flavio Cobolli.

Sinner won last year's ATP Finals, defeating Carlos Alcaraz in the final.

It was the Italian's second consecutive triumph at the event.

Frances Tiafoe proves his worth once again

Tiafoe struggled to locate his best tennis throughout the 2025 season.

The American star suffered a string of underwhelming results, and his ranking suffered as a result.

Tiafoe fell to 30th in the world at the end of last year and was far from a legitimate Grand Slam contender.

Frances Tiafoe's 2026 Grand Slam results

The 30-year-old has altered that narrative in 2026, producing some of his best tennis to rise up the rankings once again.

If the American can reproduce his US Open performances in future Grand Slam events, he will most certainly be a contender for the biggest titles for many years to come.

articles.title: Inspiring story of the day: “My mom didn’t join me for the first two years. I didn’t see her for two years.” - How Maria Sharapova turned a borrowed $700, family separation into tennis immortality
articles.summary: International Sports News: Maria Sharapova’s rise from a childhood marked by money problems and a two-year separation from her mother to becoming a five-time Grand Slam champion.
articles.body: Maria Sharapova’s rise from a childhood marked by money problems and a two-year separation from her mother to becoming a five-time Grand Slam champion remains one of tennis’ most striking stories. At seven, she left Russia with her father, Yuri Sharapov, carrying only about $700 and heading to Florida to chase a tennis dream. Her mother, Yelena, could not join them because of visa restrictions. Sharapova later spoke about the loneliness of those years and how they made her tougher. That early struggle eventually led to Wimbledon glory, a career Grand Slam, the world No. 1 ranking and, in 2025, Hall of Fame recognition.How did Maria Sharapova leave Russia with only $700Sharapova was born in Nyagan, Siberia, in 1987. Her family had links to Gomel, Belarus, and her parents had moved within the Soviet Union after the Chernobyl disaster. Tennis became the path the family believed could give Maria a different future.A major turning point came when Martina Navratilova saw the young Sharapova at a tennis clinic in Moscow. Navratilova encouraged her father to take Maria to the United States for better training. Yuri Sharapov took the advice seriously, even though the family had very little money.In 1994, Yuri and seven-year-old Maria travelled to Florida with about $700 that had been borrowed from family members. They were going to pursue training in the United States, but Yelena could not travel with them because of visa restrictions. That meant Maria left Russia knowing that her mother would remain behind.The separation lasted two years. Sharapova later explained just how difficult it was to live so far away from her mother.“My mom didn’t join me for the first two years. I didn’t see her for two years. It’s very interesting looking back at it because now I’m a mother… and I cannot imagine that kind of separation. We didn’t have cell phones or FaceTime. It was just handwritten letters. But my mother put so much emphasis on what an amazing gift it was that her husband and daughter had a chance to pursue that dream in America.”What did Maria Sharapova and Yuri Sharapov face in FloridaThe move to America did not immediately mean a comfortable life or a place at a top tennis academy. When Yuri and Maria arrived in Florida, they had very little money and did not speak English.Yuri took whatever work he could find to keep his daughter’s tennis training going. Reports from Sharapova’s early career describe him taking low-paying jobs, including washing dishes, while trying to pay for Maria’s training and everyday needs. The family’s limited finances meant the first years in Florida were about survival as much as tennis.Maria was also extremely young. She was not immediately accepted for full-time training at Nick Bollettieri’s academy because of her age. She continued developing her game before IMG later backed her training and helped her enter the academy at nine.The hardest part for Maria was not only being away from her mother. She was also learning to manage life on her own while her father worked.In her account of those years, Sharapova remembered being woken late at night by older pupils and being ordered to clean their room.“Because I was so young, I used to go to bed at 8 p.m. The other tennis pupils would come in at 11 p.m. and wake me up and order me to tidy up the room and clean it… Instead of letting that depress me, I became more quietly determined and mentally tough. I never thought of quitting because I knew what I wanted. When you come from nothing and you have nothing, then it makes you very hungry and determined.”That quote also appears in the school text based on Sharapova’s story, while similar accounts of her childhood struggles have been reported over the years.How did Maria Sharapova’s family sacrifice lead to Wimbledon gloryThe two-year separation ended when Yelena was finally able to join Maria and Yuri in the United States. By then, Maria had already learned to live without the comfort of having her mother nearby.Her tennis career began to move quickly. She turned professional in 2001 at 14 and reached the top level within a few years. In 2004, at only 17, she reached the Wimbledon final and faced Serena Williams, who was the defending champion.Sharapova produced one of the biggest wins of her young career, beating Williams in straight sets to win her first Grand Slam title.The victory changed everything. The girl who had arrived in Florida with her father and limited money was suddenly a major name in world tennis.The WTA records the Wimbledon victory as the start of a career that brought Sharapova five Grand Slam titles, 36 WTA singles titles and the world No. 1 ranking. She later won the US Open in 2006, the Australian Open in 2008 and the French Open in 2012 and 2014. Those results completed the career Grand Slam.The Wimbledon win was especially personal because of what Yuri had done to keep her dream alive. Sharapova’s relationship with her father remained an important part of her tennis story. Years later, she also remembered how much his support had shaped her career.“My dad gave up his life for me. He left his home, his country, and his wife for two years so that I could have a shot. When I climbed up that box at Wimbledon, it was to tell him that every single sacrifice he made, every dish he washed, and every tear we cried was worth it.”Why does Maria Sharapova’s childhood story still matter todaySharapova’s career eventually became much bigger than the Wimbledon victory. She reached world No. 1 in 2005 and stayed there for 21 weeks according to the WTA’s career records. She won five major titles across all four Grand Slam tournaments before retiring in 2020.But the part of her story that still stands out is what happened before the trophies. She was a young girl in a new country, separated from her mother and watching her father work to keep her tennis dream alive. She had to learn independence early, while tennis gave her a clear goal.Her career later gave that gamble a remarkable ending. In August 2025, Sharapova was officially inducted into the International Tennis Hall of Fame, adding another major honour to a career that had already included five Grand Slam titles and a career Grand Slam.Her story is therefore not simply about winning Wimbledon at 17. It is about the years before anyone knew her name, when a father and daughter arrived in America with very little money, a mother remained thousands of miles away and a young Sharapova learned to keep going even when life around her was difficult.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: La OMS agradece a Zverev su visibilización de la diabetes en la élite: "Es inspirador"
articles.standfirst: El director general de la organización médica felicitó al tenista por su victoria en el US Open y le dio las gracias por "demostrar que la diabetes no tiene que limitar los sueños de uno"
articles.summary: El director general de la organización médica felicitó al tenista por su victoria en el US Open y le dio las gracias por "demostrar que la diabetes no tiene que limitar los sueños de uno"
articles.body: En el discurso posterior a su victoria en el US Open, Alexander Zverev dedicó unas emotivas palabras a su madre y al apoyo que le ha brindado en su carrera desde que le diagnosticaron diabetes a los cuatro años. "Cuando a tu hijo de cuatro años le diagnostican diabetes y los médicos en el consultorio te dicen que su vida y el deporte van a estar sumamente limitados, se necesita una madre muy fuerte para salir de ahí y decir: 'Mi hijo será lo que él quiera ser', aseguró Zverev, tras imponerse en la final a Shelton, por 6-3, 7-6, 5-7 y 6-2. Ese mensaje que dirigió el tenista alemán a millones de espectadores ha recibido el agradecimiento de la Organización Mundial de la Salud (OMS). Su presidente, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, felicitó a Alexander por el título del US Open, su segundo Grand Slam tras Roland Garros, y por visibilizar su enfermedad, algo que puede servir de inspiración a muchas personas. "Gracias por demostrar que la diabetes no tiene que limitar los sueños de uno, y por usar tu plataforma para inspirar a otros", aseguró Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, que también hizo un llamamiento los gobiernos para fomentar la prevención. "Hago un llamado a todos los países para que inviertan en la prevención de la diabetes, el diagnóstico temprano, el tratamiento y la atención, para que todos puedan vivir una vida saludable y plena y perseguir sus sueños".

articles.body: El equipo español de Copa Davis prepara ya en Chile la eliminatoria que disputa este fin de semana y que dará el billete para la 'Final 8' de Bolonia. Rafael Jódar, Daniel Mérida, Jaume Munar y Martín Landaluce se entrenaron el lunes en la Court Central Anita Lizana de Santiago. La delegación española viajó el domingo al completo, con la única ausencia de Pedro Martínez, que se incorporará al equipo este martes tras disputar la final del ATP Challenger de Génova el pasado domingo. También ha viajado Sergio Planella como sparring del equipo. El seleccionador nacional, David Ferrer, aseguró que "ha sido un día de adaptación para los jugadores porque aquí en Santiago hay cambio de horario, jetlag, cambio de altura… y mañana ya intentaremos ser más intensos. Las sensaciones han sido buenas, la pista está bastante bien cuidada y hemos tenido todas las facilidades de la organización”. Además, Ferrer valoró la incorporación de nuevos jugadores al equipo, en el que no se encuentra Carlos Alcaraz. "Como capitán me gusta que haya jugadores jóvenes que vayan creciendo, tanto personal como tenísticamente, y más con estos jugadores que llevan un grandísimo año. Estamos hablando de Rafa Jódar, que ya está 'top-10' en el Race, o Dani Mérida, que también está ganando muchos partidos y es un jugador a destacar porque ha ido cada año mejorando su tenis".

articles.title: Sinner vuelve a entrenarse en Montecarlo tras su lesión de rodilla
articles.standfirst: Su objetivo es estar a punto para la gira asiática
articles.summary: Su objetivo es estar a punto para la gira asiática
articles.body: Jannik Sinner, número uno del mundo, volvió a entrenarse este martes en Montecarlo después de varias semanas apartado de la competición por una lesión en la rodilla derecha que le obligó a perderse los torneos de Montreal, Cincinnati y el Abierto de Estados Unidos. Sinner, que no disputa un partido oficial desde que ganó Wimbledon el pasado 12 de julio, compartió pista con el joven francés Hugo Jathiere, alumno del Piatti Tennis Center, la academia del que fuera su entrenador Riccardo Piatti. "Es un verdadero placer volver a ver a Jannik en pista y compartir este momento con él", señaló la academia en sus redes sociales al informar de la sesión. El tenista de San Cándido siguió un proceso de recuperación en las últimas semanas y pasó por el J Medical de Turín para tratar la inflamación, antes de someterse a nuevos exámenes médicos en Milán. El italiano se mantuvo alejado de la competición desde Wimbledon, que conquistó, debido a las molestias en la rodilla derecha. El pasado 9 de agosto explicó que el dolor continuaba y que todavía no estaba preparado para regresar, mientras que el 21 de agosto confirmó su baja para el Abierto de Estados Unidos al considerar que necesitaba más tiempo para recuperarse. Su objetivo es llegar en condiciones a la gira asiática, con el ATP 500 de Pekín, que comenzará el 30 de septiembre, como una de las principales fechas previstas para su regreso. También está inscrito en el Masters 1000 de Shanghái.

articles.title: Jack Draper will be sidelined from tennis for the rest of the year as he rules out returning before 2027
articles.summary: Jack Draper's injury woes continue as he rules out a return to action until 2027; the British star has not been able to play in any Grand Slam tournaments this year; "a complicated injury made things incredibly challenging," Draper admitted
articles.body:
In an emotional Instagram post, Draper said he won't be able to play again until 2027.

"Don't usually love lots of words on here but I wanted to update you that I am aiming to return to the tour at the start of 2027," Draper stated.

"Last summer all the dedication and work I had put into this sport was coming together. It was all going my way and the path seemed so clear.

"However a complicated injury made things incredibly challenging and since that moment I've been desperately trying to get back and feel as I once did on the court. Managing so much change, adversity and pain has helped me to grow massively in many areas of my life but has also made me feel a level of fatigue."

He added: "I am taking this time to reset and heal so when I return I am 100% ready to go.

"Tennis is my purpose and passion and so when I step back on court I want to make sure that there's nothing holding me back from where I want to go.

"I really appreciate all the continued support from my sponsors and people who enjoy following my tennis and I look forward to being back on court to give it my all next year."

Draper could not enter the US Open this year as he continued to struggle with a bone bruise in his dominant left arm.

The former world No 4, who has not played at a single Grand Slam this year, said he was in a "difficult place" after his first-round defeat by Martin Landaluce in the Cincinnati Open in August, admitting he was struggling to escape the mental fatigue that had built up during 15 months of battling serious injury.

articles.title: Jack Draper decides not to play again this season
articles.summary: Former world number four Jack Draper will not play again this season, but says he is aiming to return to the tour at the start of next year.
articles.body:
Former world number four Jack Draper will not play again this season, but says he is aiming to return to the tour at the start of next year.

The 24-year-old has been suffering with bone bruising in his serving arm and has only played nine events since last year's Wimbledon.

Draper missed the US Open, after losing in the first round in Montreal and Cincinnati last month - and was in tears during his defeat to France's Terence Atmane in Canada.

"I am taking this time to reset and heal so when I return I am 100% ready to go," Draper posted on Instagram. , external

"Tennis is my purpose and passion and so when I step back on court I want to make sure that there's nothing holding me back from where I want to go."

Why can't Draper play, and why won't surgery help?

Tearful Draper struggles during comeback defeat

Draper will not qualify for a protected ranking if he does return in January, as only those who are out for over six months are able to retain the ranking they had when they left the tour.

He is currently ranked 155, which means he would require wildcards or have to come through qualifying to play in Grand Slams and ATP Tour events.

But none of that will worry him if he is able to play freely and without so much pain.

Draper peaked at four in the world last June after winning a first Masters 1000 title in Indian Wells and finishing runner-up at another in Madrid.

"Last summer, all the dedication and work I had put into this sport was coming together," Draper added.

"It was all going my way and the path seemed so clear. However a complicated injury made things incredibly challenging, and since that moment I've been desperately trying to get back and feel as I once did on the court.

"Managing so much change, adversity and pain has helped me to grow massively in many areas of my life but has also made me feel a level of fatigue."

Draper has taken a holiday with friends in recent weeks and has been trying to aid his recovery by taking a mental break from the sport.

He is expected to make a gradual return to training over the next few weeks, as his team try to work out the principal causes of the injury.

Draper making changes as Murray remains part of team - analysis

Draper used to play with polyester strings, but has been experimenting with natural gut - which is against his instincts, but should ease the burden on his arm.

He has also started using a lighter racquet, and is making some changes to his serve. Diet is another area being examined to see if that, too, could be a contributing factor.

Andy Murray remains part of his coaching team but will do a limited number of weeks on the road, and so further assistance will be required.

Over the summer, Draper benefitted from the help of LTA coaches James Trotman (who was with him full-time as he rose into the world's top five) and Alex Lisiecki.

A permanent coach to work alongside Murray will need to be found, however, once Draper returns to the tour.

When he does, much thought will go into his schedule. Not just because the bone bruising is unlikely to have healed entirely by January, but also because of the concerns many top players have about the toll the modern game is putting on their bodies.

articles.body:
Aryna Sabalenka has come under fire for her actions after US Open final.

Upon losing the showpiece event to Elena Rybakina, Sabalenka threw her racket to the ground.

Sabalenka then congratulated her opponent before sitting on her bench.

This behaviour has drawn criticism from fans and pundits alike, including Chanda Rubin, who described Sabalenka's actions as 'not a good look' .

Andy Roddick, the 2003 US Open champion, has stepped into to defend the former world number one.

Andy Roddick defends Aryna Sabalenka from critics

"People are often looking for a reason to just be upset about something and to go Twitter finger their account. I just think that they are going to look for something," Roddick, the former world number one, said on the Served Podcast.

"I am not going to get mad at you if you break your own stuff. I don't care as long as you are gracious," he exclaimed.

"Could she do it after? Yeah, sure. Am I going to be personally offended that she broke her own thing? No.

"She has been salty in defeat before," Roddick continued, referring to Sabalenka's controversial comments after losing the 2025 Roland Garros final to Coco Gauff.

"But I do think there is a double standard. If someone walks off after losing the NBA Finals, they get criticised saying they are too happy, they are dapping up the people they lost to. No it's like 'they broke stuff'.

"It's like whatever, just let people live. The mistake she has made before is being made disrespectful and taking credit away from your opponent in a public fashion, but I don't care what you say to your team.

"As long as there is a base level of respect for who you have played and what you have done and what they've done, if you break a racket, who cares?

"I can't imagine being an adult seeing that and then going to a social media account and being like 'I can't believe she broke a racket'.

Aryna Sabalenka's 2026 WTA Tour tournament results

Roddick is absolutely correct in his assessment.

As tennis fans, we cannot expect players to act like robots devoid of emotion. These are human beings who need to express their frustrations from time to time.

Sabalenka had just lost a Grand Slam final in brutal circumstances; her reaction was completely understandable.

The Belarusian did not show any outward disrespect to her opponent, she merely let out the frustration that was building up inside her.

Aryna Sabalenka almost equals Venus Williams' unfortunate record

In 2017, tennis legend Venus Williams won 20 matches at Grand Slams without winning a major title.

According to OptaAce , only Venus has won more Women's Singles Grand Slam matches than Aryna Sabalenka in 2026 without winning a major title.

Sabalenka has won 19 matches at Grand Slams this year, yet she has been unable to win a major.

Aryna Sabalenka's Grand Slam results in 2026

Sabalenka will hope to bounce back emphatically when she begins her 2027 Grand Slam campaign next January in Melbourne.
